newsitem.title: USA: NYS Speaker sees no options in rent rule battle.
newsitem.headline: NYS Speaker sees no options in rent rule battle.

text.p: The New York State Assembly Speaker Tuesday ruled out compromises over a crucial aspect in the battle over rent rules, which has ground progress in other areas, including the budget, to a halt.

Both Gov George Pataki and Senate Majority Leader, Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, want vacancy decontrol, which lets landlords charge market rates once tenants move out, but Silver adamantly opposes the policy, saying a 1971 to 1974 experiment with it failed as landlords tried to push tenants out.
Asked about options for vacancy decontrol, Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, told reporters in Albany "There were no options out there."

In its Tuesday edition, the New York Times said the rent discussions included a couple of options, such as raising the bonus landlords get for vacant apartments and letting higher, free-market rents be charged for vacant apartments, though rent regulations then would apply if a tenant stayed in the same apartment.

Silver spoke to reporters after meeting with Bruno and Pataki, and all three lawmakers were set to resume their discussions this afternoon. Silver was not scheduled to take part in any talks from sundown on Tuesday until Thursday, due to a religious holiday.

The Senate and the Assembly were expected to hold sessions on Sunday evening. The rent regulations expire on Sunday, and Bruno has threatened to allow that to happen if the Senate, the Assembly and the Gov fail to agree a pact.
Vacancy decontrol would gradually end the system of apartment rent regulations, which mainly affect New York City, as it has 1.1 million such apartments, the biggest share in the state.

While Bruno has said he has enough votes to approve the Senate's own version of a bill, which would include vacancy decontrol yet try protect elderly, needy and disabled tenants, he told reporters earlier that he had enough votes to get a such a bill through the Senate--if he decided to go that route. "We will do whatever is responsible. I have the votes to do it, and I can do it when I need to," Bruno said. But he softened his stand somewhat, by saying he had yet to decide if he wanted to put out his own bill.

Whether Bruno could get a majority in the Senate to back his plan has been an ongoing question as some Republican Senators from New York City and other areas downstate that also have a number of rent-regulated apartments, have been fear it might hurt their chances for re-election.

Silver's impression of whether his Republican opponent could get a one-house bill approved differed. Accusing Bruno of not trying to protect anyone who lived south of Rockland County, he said: "He (Bruno) believes period, and he's basically and he's said it to me 'I may never pass a bill, you may be right, maybe I don't have the votes.'"

The Assembly Speaker also faulted Bruno and the Republican governor, who says his own proposal, which includes vacancy decontrol but which he says would protect the present tenants by creating penalities for landlords who harrass tenants, for not protecting the middle-class.

"The Senator keeps saying he's moved to the governor's position. The governor's position is just not good enough," Silver said, saying he was willing for U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato or anyone else to get involved in the dispute, and help protect the middle class from what he said was a pot of gold being created for landlords.
Pataki's proposal also seeks to protect needy, elderly and other tenants and preserve succession rights.
